newsitem.title: USA: Ahmanson says premature to raise Great Western bid.
newsitem.headline: Ahmanson says premature to raise Great Western bid.

text.p: H.F. Ahmanson & Co. Chairman Charles Rinehart said Monday it was premature for the nation's largest thrift to raise its bid for Great Western Financial, which last week agreed to merge with Washington Mutual Savings Bank.

In a meeting with financial analysts, Rinehart also said that Ahmanson's $6.1 billion bid for Great Western was financially superior to the $6.6 billion bid announced on Thursday by Great Western and Washington Mutual.

Analysts said last week that they expected Ahmanson to raise its bid. A Washington Mutual-Great Western merger would create the nation's largest savings and loan with $87.4 billion in assets. Ahmanson would strengthen its position as the largest thrift if it bought Great Western.

Rinehart labeled Washington Mutual's merger plan a "hope and pray" strategy, saying Seattle-based Washington Mutual was hoping to get aggressive cost savings and would "pray for a miracle on the revenue side."
He said the Washington Mutual-Great Western deal would hurt earnings of the merged company.
"We're committed to getting this deal done ... but only to the extent that we think the economics make sense," he said in response to questions about Ahmanson's next move.
Ahmanson Chief Financial Officer Kevin Twomey said Washington Mutual's projections were "highly aggressive."

"No one has ever attempted to do that before and for the simple reason that the two are incompatible," Twomey said, referring to claims Washington Mutual could cut costs and raise revenues in acquiring Great Western.
"The transaction (proposed by Washington Mutual) is dilutive without the revenue enhancements they claim," Twomey said.
A Great Western spokesman said Ahmanson's presentation "was a desparate and hollow attempt to justify what continues to be an inferior merger proposal and a losing proposition.
"We remain committed to the agreement with (WAMU) and we're confident it will be consummated quickly," he said.
Analysts have said Ahmanson should be able to achieve more cost savings than Washington Mutual because both Ahmanson and Great Western are based in southern California.

Rinehart said that if Ahmanson prevailed in a lawsuit seeking to overturn a "breakup fee" in the merger pact between Washington Mutual and Great Western, the money would go to the best interests of shareholders.
The Washington Mutual bid calls for it to collect up to $195 million if the deal breaks up and Great Western merges with someone else within 18 months.
Washington Mutual Chief Executive Kerry Killinger said last week that his company's earnings would be boosted by a merger with Great Western.
Rinehart said Ahmanson's plan for Great Western relied on a "simple and proven formula:" taking cost savings, generating more capital and using the excess to repurchase stock.

He said Washington Mutual was "stretching the envelope" with its projection of $340 million in cost savings in 1999 in a merger with Great Western. Ahmanson has said its proposed merger with Great Western would save $400 million a year.
